line: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 f3 e5 Nb3
teaches: When a pawn advance chases a centralised knight, choose the retreat that keeps it useful rather than the one that keeps it central. A knight dropped back to the wing that covers the squares your opponent's counterplay needs has not been driven away — it has been redeployed with the tempo already spent.
explains: The pawn has come to e5 and the knight in the centre must move. From b3 it covers a5 and c5, which are the squares Black's queenside counterplay wants, and it holds the pieces behind it on the back rank. The knight looks pushed to the edge and is standing exactly where the plan it is stopping needs to pass through.
